procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Delhi High Court refusing to grant bail to the petitioner.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Delhi High Court refused to grant bail to the petitioner (K. L. Sharma, K. K. Mohan and Mrs. Geetanjali Mohari).
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner initially filed a Special Leave Petition (Cr!.) No: 3000 of 1983, which was dismissed with a direction that the trial should proceed from day to day. The petitioner then filed a Criminal Miscellaneous Petition No. 2841 of 1984 seeking modification of the Supreme Court's earlier order, arguing that his advocates were not prepared to appear in the case from day to day. This petition was also dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the direction for a trial to proceed from day-to-day should be modified on the ground that the petitioner's advocates are not prepared to appear daily?

facts: The Court had previously directed that a criminal trial should proceed from day to day.
The petitioner filed an application to modify this direction.
The reason provided was that the petitioner's advocates were not prepared to appear in court daily, as they expected the trial to be prolonged.
law: It is the professional duty of an advocate who accepts a brief in a criminal case to attend the trial from day to day.
The practice of conducting trials from day to day is considered wholesome, expedient, and in the best interest of both the prosecution and the defense.
Day-to-day trials lead to expedition (speed) and help eliminate 'manoeuvre and mischief'.
Once a trial commences, it should proceed 'de die in diem' (from day to day) until it is concluded, except for a very pressing reason that makes an adjournment inevitable.
application: The Court was unable to appreciate the difficulty cited by the petitioner.
It framed the issue not as the petitioner's difficulty, but as the advocates' failure to fulfill their professional duty.
The Court reasoned that an advocate, having accepted the case, would be committing a breach of professional duty by failing to attend daily.
The inconvenience of the advocates was not considered a 'very pressing reason' sufficient to justify modifying the order for a continuous trial.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's request, holding that an advocate's unpreparedness to appear daily is not a valid ground to modify an order for a day-to-day trial. The Court affirmed the importance of continuous trials and the professional duty of advocates to attend them.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the direction for a trial to proceed from day-to-day should be modified on the ground that the petitioner's advocates are not prepared to appear daily?
appellant_arguments: The petitioner's two advocates are not prepared to appear in the case from day-to-day as the trial is likely to be prolonged.
The petitioner's advocate is finding it difficult to attend the court from day-to-day.
respondent_arguments: The provided text does not state the respondent's arguments.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Once a trial commences, the court must proceed from day-to-day until its conclusion, except for a very pressing reason which makes an adjournment inevitable. It is the duty of an advocate who accepts a brief in a criminal case to attend the trial from day-to-day.
obiter: It is an entirely wholesome practice for trials to proceed from day-to-day.
Conducting trials from day-to-day results in expedition and the elimination of manoeuvre and mischief.
It is in the interest of both the prosecution and the defence that the trial proceeds from day-to-day.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court finds that an advocate's difficulty or unpreparedness to appear daily is not a valid reason to modify a direction for a day-to-day trial. It is the professional duty of an advocate who accepts a criminal brief to attend the trial from day-to-day, and failing to do so constitutes a breach of that duty. The practice of continuous trials is considered wholesome and in the best interest of both the prosecution and the defense.
legal_tests_applied: Once the trial commences, a Sessions Judge should, except for a very pressing reason which makes an adjournment inevitable, proceed de die in diem until the trial is concluded.
why_appellant_lost: It is the duty of every Advocate, who accepts the brief in a criminal case to attend the trial from day-to-day.
Having accepted the brief, he will be committing a breach of his professional duty, if he so fails to attend.
The court was unable to appreciate the difficulty said to be experienced by the petitioner.
why_respondent_won: It is an entirely wholesome practice for the trial to go on from day-to-day.
It is most expedient that the trial before the court of a Session should proceed and be dealt with continuously from its inception to its finish.
It will be in the interest of both the prosecution and the defence that the trial proceeds from day-to-day.
policy_considerations: A day-to-day trial will result in expedition.
A day-to-day trial will also result in the elimination of manoeuvre and mischief.
